outcome: No resolution, partial case, or bound has been found since 26 January 2024; the problem is still open and the only relevant development is an October 2024 expository article restating the known combinatorial constraints without proving anything new.
summary: The problem asks whether a non-convex, non-self-intersecting polyhedron with more than seven faces exists in which every pair of faces shares an edge. Only two such polyhedra are known at all: the tetrahedron (f=4, genus 0) and the Szilassi polyhedron (f=7, genus 1), discovered in 1977. The triage's found item, 'Polyhedra with Every Face Connected to All Others Through Edges' (Crux Mathematicorum, Vol. 50(8), October 2024, by an author whose combinatorial derivation gives the Euler-characteristic constraint on possible (f, genus) pairs), was checked: search-engine summaries and secondary sources consistently describe it as identifying the next combinatorially admissible case (f=12, 44 vertices, 66 edges, genus 6, hendecagonal faces) as an abstract polytope, while explicitly stating that it remains unknown whether this abstract structure can be geometrically realized with planar, non-self-intersecting faces in R^3. I could not get a direct fetch of the article text (ResearchGate returned HTTP 403), so I rely on multiple independent search-result digestions of it, all of which agree on this characterization: the piece narrows the space of *candidate parameters* combinatorially but does not construct, or disprove the existence of, any new polyhedron beyond the two already known before the frozen date. This is consistent with Crux Mathematicorum's nature as a problems/exposition journal rather than a venue for new geometric-construction theorems. I separately checked the current (2026) Wikipedia articles for 'Szilassi polyhedron' and the unsolved-problems list; the Szilassi polyhedron article's most recent citation is the 2024 journal version of Arseneva et al., 'Adjacency Graphs of Polyhedral Surfaces' (Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2024; conference version SoCG 2021, arXiv 2103.09803) — but that paper addresses realizability of arbitrary adjacency graphs as polyhedral surfaces in general, not this specific all-pairs-adjacent, more-than-seven-faces question, and its results predate the frozen revision in any case (SoCG 2021), so even if it were on-topic it would not constitute a change in the window. No arXiv preprint, blog post, or announcement was found claiming a geometric realization of the f=12 genus-6 case, nor any disproof of its existence, nor any other progress on the problem since 26 January 2024. No AI involvement of any kind was found near this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the October 2024 Crux article, by explicitly working out the next admissible (f, genus) pair (12, 6) and the associated (V, E) counts via Euler's formula, constitutes 'progress' in the sense of narrowing the search space for a case of the problem, which could support status='progress' rather than 'open'. I did not adopt this reading because the problem as stated is an existence question ('Is there a...'), and per §3.1 an existence/infinitude question is only advanced by an actual answer, not by narrowing where an answer could hide (analogous to extending a record table). Working out combinatorial admissibility constraints via Euler's formula was already implicit in the known theory before 2024 (the same constraint that produces f=4 and f=7 as the first two cases); the article appears to restate and extend this arithmetic rather than establish any new mathematical fact about realizability.
what_would_settle_it: Either an explicit geometric construction (coordinates or a combinatorial-to-geometric realization proof) of a non-convex, non-self-intersecting polyhedron with f=12 (or any other admissible f>7) faces all pairwise edge-adjacent, or a proof that no such realization exists for the genus-6 case, would settle whether progress has occurred. Direct access to the full text of the October 2024 Crux Mathematicorum article (behind the ResearchGate 403 and not otherwise located as an open PDF) would also let me confirm definitively whether it contains any such claim, rather than relying on secondary search-result summaries.
